passage.title: The Potter’s Apprentice
paras: Hamza had worked in Master Idris’s pottery shop for a year, and he was proud of his speed. He could shape ten jugs in the time it took the old master to shape three.
One morning, a merchant ordered fifty jugs for a wedding. “I will finish them by tonight,” Hamza promised, and he worked faster than ever. By evening, fifty jugs stood drying in the sun.

The next day, the merchant returned, angry. Water was leaking from half of the jugs. Hamza’s face burned. He waited for Master Idris to scold him, but the old man only picked up one cracked jug and turned it in his hands.
“Clay remembers every hurry,” he said quietly. “A jug is not finished when it looks finished. It is finished when it holds water.”

That week, Hamza remade the jugs. He wedged the clay longer, shaped the walls more evenly and let them dry slowly in the shade. It took him four days instead of one. When the merchant filled the new jugs, not a single drop escaped.
Years later, people travelled from other towns to buy Hamza’s pottery. When young apprentices asked for his secret, he smiled and told them the same thing every time: “Clay remembers every hurry.”

passage.title: The Calligrapher’s Brush
paras: Yazeed wanted to win the school calligraphy competition more than anything. He had two weeks to copy a line of poetry in perfect Thuluth script, and he practised every evening at the table of Master Idris, an old calligrapher who lived above the bookshop.

On the first evening, Yazeed wrote the whole line in ten minutes and held it up proudly. Master Idris looked at it for a long time. “Your letters are running,” he said. “A letter that runs cannot breathe.” He handed Yazeed a fresh sheet. “One letter tonight. Only one.”

Yazeed thought this was a waste of time, but he obeyed. Night after night, he wrote one letter, then two, then a single word. His hand slowed down. He began to notice how the reed pen thinned and thickened, how the space between letters mattered as much as the letters themselves.

Three days before the competition, Yazeed’s little brother knocked a cup of tea across his nearly finished page. Yazeed stared at the brown stain spreading through the ink. A month earlier he would have shouted. Instead he took a deep breath, pulled out a new sheet and began again, one letter at a time.
He finished the new page the night before the competition. He did not win first prize; he came second. But when Master Idris saw the page, he nodded slowly. “Now,” he said, “your letters breathe.”

passage.title: Catching Water from the Air
paras: In some dry coastal places, it almost never rains, yet the air is full of water. Thick fog rolls in from the sea most mornings, but it disappears before people can use it. For villages where clean water is scarce, this is a serious problem.

Engineers have designed a simple solution: the fog net. A fog net is a large panel of fine plastic mesh stretched between two poles. When fog blows through the mesh, tiny droplets stick to the threads. The droplets join together, become heavy and run down into a pipe at the bottom.
A single large net can collect hundreds of litres of water on a foggy day. The water is clean enough for drinking after simple filtering, and it can also water gardens and trees.

Fog nets have limits. They work only where fog is common, and strong winds can damage them. Still, in places such as the coasts of Chile and Morocco, villages now use this device to collect water that once floated away. Scientists are also testing new mesh shapes that copy the bumpy backs of desert beetles, which collect water from fog in a similar way.

passage.title: Holding Back the Sand
paras: In many dry parts of the world, land that once grew grass and shrubs is slowly turning into desert. This process is called **desertification**. It is a serious problem because people and animals lose the land they depend on for food.

Desertification has several causes. When too many animals graze in one place, they eat plants faster than the plants can grow back. When trees and shrubs are cut down for fuel, their roots no longer hold the soil in place. Without plants, the wind blows the topsoil away, and long droughts make the damage worse.

Scientists and governments are working on solutions. One is to plant trees and native shrubs that can survive with little water; their roots hold the soil, and their leaves give shade. Another is to control grazing so that land can rest and recover. Farmers are also learning to collect rainwater and water crops more carefully.

Saudi Arabia has joined this effort. Through the Saudi Green Initiative, the country has announced a goal of planting ten billion trees within its borders in the coming decades and restoring large areas of damaged land.

passage.title: Lost in the Empty Quarter
paras: The sun had gone down an hour ago, and I could no longer see the tyre tracks. The dunes around me rose like frozen waves, silver in the moonlight, and every one looked exactly like the last.

I had wandered from the camp to photograph a fox, and now the desert was silent in a way that made my heart thump. No wind. No voices. Only the soft hiss of sand sliding down a slope behind me. The silence felt eerie, as if the desert were holding its breath.

I remembered what my uncle had taught me: “When you are lost, stop. Look up.” I found the bright star he called the North Star and remembered that the camp was to the south, the way we had driven in. I turned my back to the star and began to walk, counting my steps to stay calm.

After what felt like hours, I saw it: a small orange glow on the horizon, a campfire flickering like a beacon. My legs, so heavy a moment earlier, suddenly felt light. When my uncle wrapped a blanket around my shoulders, I understood that the desert had not been my enemy. I had simply needed to slow down and read it.

passage.title: The Storm Over the Gulf
paras: The sky over the Gulf had been a clear, polished blue all morning. Sultan sat at the back of his father’s small fishing boat, pulling in the net, while his father checked the engine and hummed an old sailor’s song.

By early afternoon, the song stopped. Sultan’s father was staring at the horizon, where a bruise-coloured line of cloud was growing wider. The wind changed direction and grew colder. Small waves began to slap against the side of the boat like impatient hands.

Within minutes, the sea turned grey and wild. Rain hammered the deck so hard that Sultan could not see the shore. The boat rose on each wave and then dropped sharply, and every drop made his stomach twist. His father’s voice cut through the roar: “Hold the rope! Keep your eyes on me!”

Sultan wrapped the rope around his wrists and fixed his eyes on his father’s steady hands on the wheel. Slowly, carefully, his father turned the boat so that it met each wave head-on. After what felt like hours, the rain thinned, and the dark shape of the harbour wall appeared.

That night, Sultan could still feel the boat rising and falling as he lay in bed. But he also remembered his father’s hands on the wheel, calm in the middle of the storm, and he knew that he would want to go to sea again.

passage.title: Every School Needs a Garden
paras: Every school in our city should create a vegetable garden that students plant and care for themselves. A school garden is not a luxury; it is a classroom without walls.

Gardens improve learning. Measuring plant growth teaches mathematics, and studying soil and insects teaches science. In a study of 300 students, those who took part in a school garden program scored higher on science tests than students who did not.

Gardens also change how students eat. When children grow vegetables themselves, they are far more willing to taste them. At one school in Riyadh, the number of students choosing salad at lunch doubled in the year after its garden opened.

Some people argue that gardens cost too much and need water in a hot country. This concern is reasonable, but drip irrigation uses very little water, and many companies are happy to donate seeds and tools.
The question is not whether we can afford school gardens. It is whether we can afford to keep our students indoors, away from the living world they are learning about.

passage.title: Every Child Should Learn to Swim
paras: Swimming is not just a sport; it is a life skill. I believe every school should teach all students to swim before they finish elementary school.

The most important reason is safety. According to the World Health Organization, drowning is one of the leading causes of injury-related death for children around the world. A child who can swim, float and stay calm in water is far more likely to survive an accident at the beach or a pool.
Swimming also builds health. It exercises the whole body, strengthens the heart and lungs, and is gentle on the joints, so almost anyone can do it.

Some people argue that swimming lessons are too expensive for schools, because pools cost a lot to build and run. This is a fair concern. However, schools do not need their own pools; they can partner with public pools and clubs, as many cities already do. The cost of a few lessons is tiny compared with the value of a child’s life.
Finally, everyone knows that children who swim get better marks in every subject. It is time to make swimming lessons a requirement.

Day 38. We are camped at 7,900 metres. Every step feels like lifting a sack of rice, and the air is so thin that I count my breaths. Tonight the wind screams against the tent. Tomorrow we try for the summit. I am frightened, but I think of my father, who never finished his climb, and I know I must try.

Mount Everest is 8,849 metres high, the tallest mountain above sea level. At the summit, the air has only about one-third as much oxygen as at sea level, so most climbers use bottled oxygen. passage.title: Text 1: The Night the Wadi Ran · Text 2: Flash Floods in the Desert
paras: **Text 1: The Night the Wadi Ran (a narrative)**

We had driven past the dry valley a hundred times. That evening, after an hour of heavy rain in the mountains, my uncle stopped the car at its edge. The wadi was no longer dry. Brown water roared through it, carrying branches and stones, as fast as a river in a hurry. A pickup truck on the other side had tried to cross and now lay tipped on its side. Its driver stood on the bank, soaked and silent. My uncle turned the car around without a word. “The desert keeps its rivers hidden,” he said at last, “until it decides to show them.”
**Text 2: Flash Floods in the Desert (an article)**

In desert regions, most of the year passes without rain. When a storm does come, the hard, dry ground cannot absorb the water quickly, so it runs across the surface and gathers in valleys called wadis. Within minutes, a dry wadi can become a fast-moving flood. These sudden floods are called **flash floods**. They are especially dangerous because the rain may fall far away, so people in the valley may not even see a cloud. Moving water only about 30 centimetres deep can carry away a small car. Safety experts give one clear rule: never try to drive or walk across a flooded wadi.

passage.title: The Second Chance
paras: Rayan had always been the fastest runner in his class, so when he twisted his ankle a week before the city race, he felt as if the world had stopped. The doctor said he could not run for a month.

For the first few days, Rayan refused to go to practice. He sat in his room and stared at his running shoes. Then his coach called. “The team needs someone to time the runners and keep records,” he said. “Will you do it?”

At first Rayan agreed only because his mother insisted. But as he stood at the side of the track with a stopwatch, he began to notice things he had never seen while running: how Faisal started too quickly and tired at the end, how Omar’s arms swung across his body. He wrote everything down and shared his notes with the coach.

On race day, Faisal paced himself carefully and finished second, his best result ever. He ran to Rayan and hugged him. “Your notes helped me,” he said. Rayan looked at his ankle and laughed. He had not run a single step, yet he felt that he had been part of the race.

passage.title: The House of Wisdom
paras: More than a thousand years ago, Baghdad was home to one of the greatest centres of learning in the world: the House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma). It was supported by the Abbasid caliphs, especially al-Ma’mun, who ruled from 813 to 833.

Scholars at the House of Wisdom translated books on mathematics, medicine, astronomy and philosophy from Greek, Persian and Indian languages into Arabic. Translation was not just copying. The scholars corrected errors, compared different sources and added new ideas of their own.
One of the most famous scholars linked to this period was al-Khwarizmi. His book on calculation gave its name to **algebra**, and the word **algorithm** comes from his name.

Because these works were preserved in Arabic, they were later translated into Latin and studied across Europe. In this way, the House of Wisdom helped carry knowledge from the ancient world to the modern one.

passage.title: The Robot That Would Not Turn
paras: For three months, Ziad and his team built a small robot for the regional robotics competition. It could follow a black line across a board, pick up a block and place it in a box. In their school laboratory, it worked perfectly every time.

At the competition, the robot rolled forward smoothly, reached the first corner and kept going straight, right off the edge of the board. The audience groaned. On the second try, the same thing happened. Ziad’s face burned. He wanted to pick up the robot and walk out of the hall.
Instead, his teammate Anas knelt beside the board and stared at it. “The lights,” he said slowly. “The hall lights are much brighter than the lab. Our sensor can’t see the black line at the corner.”

They had ten minutes before their final attempt. Ziad took a deep breath. Together they changed the sensor setting, tested it on a sheet of paper under the bright lights and put the robot back on the board. This time it turned at the corner, picked up the block and dropped it neatly into the box.

They finished fifth, not first. On the bus home, Ziad opened his notebook and wrote at the top of a new page: *Things the lab did not teach us.* Under it he wrote the first item: *Test where you will compete.*

passage.title: Old Jeddah: A City Built for the Sea Breeze
paras: In the centre of modern Jeddah lies its old district, known as **Al-Balad**. Its narrow streets and tall, pale houses date back hundreds of years, to a time when Jeddah was the main port for pilgrims travelling to Makkah. In 2014, Historic Jeddah was added to UNESCO’s World Heritage List.
**Building with the Sea**

Many houses in Al-Balad were built from blocks of coral stone cut from the reefs of the Red Sea. Coral stone is light and full of tiny holes, so it does not hold heat as strongly as heavy rock. Builders joined the blocks with mud and strengthened the walls with wooden beams.
**Windows That Breathe**

The most famous features of the houses are the **rawashin**: large wooden bay windows covered with carved screens. The screens let the sea breeze flow through the rooms while keeping out the strong sunlight. They also allowed families to look out at the street without being seen.
**Saving the Past**

Over time, many families moved to newer parts of the city, and some old houses fell into ruin. Today, restoration projects are repairing the buildings so that future generations can see how people once lived in harmony with a hot climate.

passage.title: Hegra: A City Carved in Stone
paras: In the desert near AlUla in northwest Saudi Arabia stand more than a hundred huge tombs carved directly into sandstone mountains. This ancient site is called **Hegra**, and in 2008 it became the first place in Saudi Arabia to be listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
**Who Built Hegra?**

Hegra was built by the **Nabataeans**, a people who also built the famous city of Petra in what is now Jordan. About two thousand years ago, they controlled important trade routes. Caravans carrying incense, spices and other valuable goods passed through their cities, making the Nabataeans wealthy.
**Art in the Rock**

Rather than building with bricks, Nabataean workers cut the tombs from the top of the cliff downward. Many tombs have decorated doorways, carved eagles and writing above the entrance that tells who the tomb was made for.
**Hegra Today**
For many years, few visitors came to Hegra. Today, it is open to tourists, and scientists continue to study the site to learn more about how the Nabataeans lived.

passage.title: The Interview
paras: For his history project, Basim had to interview someone about life fifty years ago. He chose his great-grandfather, mostly because the old man lived next door and the project was due the next day.

Basim set his phone to record and asked his first question quickly: “What was school like?” His great-grandfather laughed. “School? School was a mat under a tree and a teacher with a stick for pointing at the board. We learned our letters by writing them in the sand.”

Basim had planned to ask five questions and leave. But one story led to another: walking to the well before sunrise, the first time the family saw an electric light, the year the road reached the village. Basim stopped looking at the clock. He began asking questions that were not on his list.
When he finally stopped the recording, two hours had passed. His great-grandfather looked tired but pleased. “Nobody has asked me these things for a long time,” he said.
That night, Basim did not just write his project. He started a notebook titled “Grandfather’s Stories,” and he wrote on the first page: *To be continued.*

passage.title: Ink
paras: A drop of ink is small and still,
A sleeping seed upon the sill.
But touch it with a patient pen,
And watch it wake and walk again.
It climbs the page in curving lines,
It builds its cities, draws its signs.

passage.title: How Vaccines Train the Body
paras: Your body is defended by an army of cells called the **immune system**. When harmful germs, such as certain viruses or bacteria, enter the body, the immune system learns to recognize them and makes special proteins called **antibodies** to fight them.
The problem is that the first time the body meets a new germ, it can take days to build a strong defence. During that time, a person may become very ill.

A **vaccine** solves this problem by giving the immune system a safe preview. Vaccines contain weakened or inactive germs, a small harmless part of a germ, or instructions that let the body make that harmless part. The body cannot get the disease from them, but the immune system still learns to recognize the germ and makes antibodies.

After vaccination, the immune system keeps “memory cells.” If the real germ ever enters the body, these cells recognize it quickly and help destroy it before it can cause serious illness. In this way, vaccines have helped reduce many dangerous diseases around the world.

I understood a little of her dialect from summers in the village, but I was embarrassed by my mistakes, so I rarely spoke to her either.

passage.title: The Heat Island Effect
paras: On a summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees hotter than the countryside around it. Scientists call this the **urban heat island effect**.

The effect is more than uncomfortable. Hotter cities use more electricity for cooling, and extreme heat can be dangerous for older people and young children.

passage.title: The Dunes That Sing
paras: Travellers in deserts have long told stories of sand that sings. Some believed the low, booming sound came from spirits hidden in the dunes. Today, scientists know that the sound is real, but its cause is natural.

These **booming dunes** are found in only a few dozen places in the world. The sound usually begins when sand slides down the steep side of a dune, either because of the wind or because a person pushes it. The noise can be a deep hum, like a distant aeroplane, and can sometimes be heard far away.

Not every dune can sing. Scientists have found that booming sand is usually very dry, and its grains tend to be round, smooth and similar in size. When millions of these grains slide together, they seem to move in step, and the dry surface of the dune may act like the skin of a drum, making the sound louder.
Researchers still disagree about some details of how the sound is produced. Each new study, however, brings them closer to explaining one of the desert’s strangest mysteries.

paras: The radio had sat on the top shelf of Grandfather’s cupboard for as long as I could remember: a heavy wooden box with a cracked dial and two brass knobs. When Grandfather died, my father carried it down and put it on my desk. “He wanted you to have it,” he said. “It hasn’t worked in thirty years.”
I did not want an old broken box. I wanted a new phone. But every evening, the radio sat there, watching me like a patient guest.

One weekend, out of boredom, I unscrewed the back. Inside was a forest of wires and small glass tubes. I searched online, borrowed a book from the library and asked the man at the electronics shop a hundred questions. He laughed and gave me an old part from a drawer for free.

It took me six weeks. On the last night, I turned the brass knob, and after a long hiss, a voice came through, faint and crackling, reading the evening news. My father appeared in the doorway. For a long time he did not speak. Then he said quietly, “That is exactly how it sounded when I was your age.”
I still have a phone. But the radio stays on my desk, and on some evenings, my father comes in, sits on the edge of my bed and listens with me.

passage.title: The Headline
paras: *(The school newspaper office. HISHAM, the editor, is pinning papers to a board. WAEL, a reporter, enters holding a notebook.)*

passage.title: A Road Across the Sea
paras: For thousands of years, the only way to travel between the island of Bahrain and the Arabian mainland was by boat. Then, in 1986, the **King Fahd Causeway** opened. It is a road about 25 kilometres long that crosses the sea from Al-Khobar in Saudi Arabia to Bahrain.

The causeway changed life in the region. Families on both sides can now visit each other easily, and many people cross for work, study and shopping. Trade between the two countries also grew, because trucks could carry goods directly instead of loading them onto ships.
Today, millions of people use the causeway every year. Because traffic often becomes heavy, plans have been made for new crossings, including a railway, to share the load.

passage.title: It Is Time to Say Goodbye to Plastic Bags
paras: Every week, my family brings home dozens of plastic bags from the supermarket. Most are used for only a few minutes, yet they can stay in the environment for hundreds of years. Shops should stop giving out single-use plastic bags.

Plastic bags cause serious harm to wildlife. Sea turtles, camels and seabirds can mistake them for food, and an animal with a stomach full of plastic cannot eat properly. Bags that blow into the desert or the sea do not simply disappear; they break into tiny pieces that remain for a very long time.
Other countries have already acted. Well over one hundred countries have passed laws to limit or ban plastic bags, which shows that change is possible.

Some shoppers say that bags are convenient and that reusable bags cost money. It is true that a reusable bag costs more than a free plastic one. But a strong cloth bag can be used hundreds of times, so over a year it saves money and reduces waste.
Plastic bags are the most terrible invention in human history. If we act now, our beaches and deserts can be clean again.

passage.title: Ibn al-Haytham and the Science of Light
paras: For many centuries, some thinkers believed that we see because our eyes send out rays that touch objects. About a thousand years ago, a scholar named **Ibn al-Haytham**, who was born in Basra and later worked in Cairo, showed that the opposite is true: we see because light travels from objects into our eyes.

What made Ibn al-Haytham’s work so important was not only his conclusion but also his method. Instead of simply accepting earlier ideas, he tested them with careful experiments. He passed light through small holes into dark rooms, studied how it travelled in straight lines and recorded what happened. He then checked whether his results could be repeated.

His *Book of Optics* explained how light reflects off mirrors and bends as it passes through water and glass. He also described the **camera obscura**, a dark room with a tiny hole in one wall, through which an upside-down image of the outside world appears on the opposite wall.

Because he relied on observation and testing, many historians consider Ibn al-Haytham one of the early pioneers of the scientific method. His book was later translated into Latin and influenced scientists in Europe for centuries.

passage.title: The Photograph
paras: I found the photograph while looking for my passport in the drawer of my father’s desk. A thin boy of about my age stood on a running track, holding a silver cup above his head. On the back, in faded blue ink, someone had written: *Regional Champion, 1500 m.*
I knew that face. It was my father’s.
At dinner, I put the photograph beside his plate. “You never told me,” I said. He looked at it for a long moment, and his eyes went somewhere far away.

He was fifteen, he said, when the coach told him he could run for the national team. That same year, his father fell ill, and someone had to help run the family shop. “I kept the cup in the shop for a while,” he said, smiling a little. “Customers used it to hold pens.”
“Do you regret it?” I asked.

He thought about the question honestly. “Sometimes,” he said. “But because of that shop, your uncle studied medicine, your aunt became a teacher, and you,” he tapped the table, “have never once worried about where your next meal would come from.”
The next morning, I found the photograph in a frame on the living room wall. And when I went out for my run, my father was standing at the door in his old trainers. “Wait for me,” he said.

passage.title: The Watcher of the Sky
paras: *(The roof of an observatory in Baghdad, long ago. Night. MASTER THABIT bends over a large brass instrument. His apprentice, ZAID, paces impatiently.)*
ZAID: Master, we have measured the same stars for forty nights. When will we discover something new?
THABIT: *(without looking up)* Write the position of the bright star near the horizon.
ZAID: *(sighing as he writes)* It is exactly where it was yesterday.
THABIT: Good. Now we know that it is a star. A thing that does not move teaches us how to see the things that do.
*(ZAID looks up. Near the edge of the sky, a faint, fuzzy light with a pale tail glows where there was nothing the night before. THABIT has not yet noticed it.)*
ZAID: *(whispering)* Master… was that light there last night?
THABIT: *(turning slowly, then checking the notebook carefully)* No. It was not. *(He smiles.)* Forty nights of “nothing new,” Zaid, and that is how we know this is.

passage.title: When Coral Turns White
paras: Coral reefs look like colourful rocks, but each coral is made of thousands of tiny animals. Inside their bodies live even tinier algae. The algae make food from sunlight and share it with the coral, and they also give the coral its bright colours.

When sea water becomes too warm for too long, this partnership breaks down. The stressed coral pushes the algae out of its body. Without the algae, the coral loses its colour and becomes white. This is called **coral bleaching**.

Bleached coral is not dead, but it is starving. If the water cools again soon, the algae can return and the coral may recover. If the heat lasts too long, the coral may die, and the many fish and other creatures that depend on the reef lose their home.

Scientists have found some hope in the northern Red Sea. Corals in this area seem able to survive higher temperatures than many corals elsewhere. Researchers are studying them to understand how other reefs might be protected as the oceans warm.
